evidence_set: 9 healthy volunteers with earlier ecstasy use (7 men, 2 women; 2 to 300 occasions), double blind, MDMA 0.75 and 1.5 mg/kg in ascending order and placebo placed at random among the sessions. In the scanner they saw blocks of happy, neutral, angry, fearful, disgusted and sad faces and rated each expression as unpleasant, neutral or pleasant with a button box. Accuracy of these ratings, as marginal means across all the facial expressions (standard error), was 0.89 (0.04), 0.91 (0.01) and 0.86 (0.02) on placebo, 0.75 and 1.5 mg/kg (F(2,16) 0.9); reaction time was 1,345.7 (45.6), 1,168.9 (79.5) and 1,292.3 (115.5), the unit printed as microseconds (F(2,16) 3.1). Neither test is marked significant, nor is the drug-by-emotion-type interaction for accuracy (F(10,80) 1.2) or reaction time (F(10,80) 0.6); the text says MDMA did not affect the accuracy of emotion recognition or reaction time. Editors' calculation: degrees of freedom of 10 and 80 fit six kinds of faces in 9 people, so the disgusted and sad faces, which the Methods say were not used in the analyses, appear to be included in these means; F(2,16) 3.1 gives p of about .07.
